theory_refs.why: The two trigger words for opposite-end pointers.

theory_refs.at: Binary search per element → one combined walk
theory_refs.why: Why r only ever moves left.

theory_refs.at: Move l when the sum is too small

stages.title: Understand
stages.body:
✍️ f(sorted array a (1-indexed answer), target) → [i, j] with i < j and a[i] + a[j] = target. Exactly one answer. Must use O(1) extra space.
- n ≤ 3·10⁴.
- [2, 7, 11, 15], target 9 → [1, 2].

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ Same question as Two Sum, but sorted and with a space limit — the space limit rules out yesterday's map.
✍️ By hand: 2 + 15 = 17 is too big. Is 15 useful with anything? Its smallest partner is 2, already too big → 15 is useless. Drop it.
✍️ Hard part: trusting that dropping an element can never lose the answer.
✍️ Edges: negative numbers; the answer is the two end elements; equal values.

stages.title: Brainstorm: brute → optimal
stages.body:
✍️ **1. Brute.** All pairs. O(n²).
✍️ **2. Better.** For each i, binary search target − a[i] in a[i+1..]. O(n log n), O(1).
✍️ ↳ Bottleneck: each search restarts from scratch, but as a[i] grows its partner can only get smaller.
✍️ **3. Hash map.** O(n) time but O(n) space — breaks the requirement.
✍️ **4. Optimal.** l = 0, r = n−1. Sum too small → only a bigger left element can help → l++. Too big → r--. O(n), O(1).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body:
✍️ 1. Start with one pointer at each end.
✍️ 2. While they have not met, add the two values.
✍️ 3. Equal to target → return the 1-based indices.
✍️ 4. Smaller → move the left pointer right. Larger → move the right pointer left.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
STATE   l = 0; r = n-1
LOOP    while l < r
CHECK     s = a[l] + a[r]
          if s == target: return [l+1, r+1]
UPDATE    if s < target: l++   else: r--
RETURN  []
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Edge cases and complexity
stages.body:
✍️ O(n) time, O(1) space.
✍️ 1-based output — easy to forget.
- Sum of two values ≤ 1000 in magnitude here, so no overflow; use `long long` in variants.

stages.title: Carry forward
stages.body:
✍️ Unsorted + indices → hash map. Sorted (or sortable when indices don't matter) + O(1) space → two pointers.
✍️ Every pointer move must be justified by "the discarded element cannot be in a valid answer".

stages.title: Interview follow-ups
stages.body:
- *Count all pairs with sum < target.* When a[l] + a[r] < target, all r − l pairs (l, l+1..r) qualify ([[tp-opposite-ends#variations]]).
- *Pair with the closest sum.* Track min |s − target| while moving the same way.
- *Why is binary search per element worse?* O(n log n) vs O(n); it ignores that the partner moves monotonically.

siblings.title: Squares of a Sorted Array
siblings.maps: The biggest square is always at one of the two ends — two pointers fill the output from the back.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ Sorted (may contain negatives); return the squares in sorted order in O(n).
✍️ Brute: square and sort → O(n log n).

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Bottleneck: sorting, although the squares are "large at both ends, small in the middle". The largest remaining square is at l or r → write it at the end of the output and move that pointer.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ l = 0, r = n−1, write = n−1; compare |a[l]| and |a[r]|; put the larger square at out[write], move that pointer, write--.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
l = 0; r = n-1
for w from n-1 down to 0:
    if |a[l]| > |a[r]|: out[w] = a[l]^2; l++
    else: out[w] = a[r]^2; r--
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Two ends hold the extremes of a sorted array — the basis of every opposite-end scan ([[tp-opposite-ends#variations]]).

siblings.title: Reverse String
siblings.maps: The simplest opposite-ends loop: swap and move both pointers.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Reverse a char array in place, O(1) extra.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Swap a[l] and a[r], l++, r−−, until they meet.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Swap the outermost pair, then the next pair inwards, until the middle.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
l = 0; r = n-1
while l < r: swap(a[l], a[r]); l++; r--
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Symmetric processing = opposite ends ([[tp-opposite-ends#palindrome]]).

siblings.title: Count Pairs Whose Sum is Less than Target
siblings.maps: Sort first (indices don't matter for a count), then count r − l pairs at once.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Count pairs i < j with a[i] + a[j] < target.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Brute O(n²). The count does not depend on positions → sort. If a[l] + a[r] < target, then a[l] pairs with every index l+1..r → add r − l, l++. Else r−−.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Sort; opposite ends; add a block of pairs whenever the sum is small enough.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
sort a; l = 0; r = n-1; cnt = 0
while l < r:
    if a[l] + a[r] < target: cnt += r - l; l++
    else: r--
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Counting with two pointers adds a whole block at once — the trick reused in Valid Triangle Number ([[tp-fix-one-k-sum#variations]]).

theory_refs.at: Inner skip loops also check l < r

stages.title: Understand
stages.body:
✍️ f(string) → true if, after dropping non-alphanumeric characters and ignoring case, it reads the same both ways.
- Length ≤ 2·10⁵, printable ASCII.
- "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" → true.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ By hand: compare the first letter with the last, skipping spaces and punctuation, moving inwards.
✍️ Hard part: skipping on both sides without running past each other.
✍️ Edges: empty after cleaning (e.g. " ", ".,") → true; "0P" → false (digits count).

stages.title: Brainstorm: brute → optimal
stages.body:
✍️ **1. Simple.** Build a cleaned lowercase copy, compare it with its reverse. O(n) time, O(n) space. Perfectly acceptable as a first answer.
✍️ ↳ The extra string is the only cost; the follow-up asks for O(1) space.
✍️ **2. Optimal.** Two pointers on the original string, skipping non-alphanumerics on each side, comparing lowercase forms. O(n), O(1).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body:
✍️ 1. l at the start, r at the end.
✍️ 2. Move l right past non-alphanumeric characters; move r left likewise (never crossing).
✍️ 3. If the lowercase characters differ, return false; else move both inwards.
✍️ 4. If the pointers meet, return true.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
STATE   l = 0; r = n-1
LOOP    while l < r
UPDATE    while l < r and not alnum(s[l]): l++
          while l < r and not alnum(s[r]): r--
CHECK     if lower(s[l]) != lower(s[r]): return false
UPDATE    l++; r--
RETURN  true
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Dry run
stages.body:
"race a car" → cleaned "raceacar":
| l char | r char | equal? |
|---|---|---|
| r | r | yes |
| a | a | yes |
| c | c | yes |
| e | a | no → false |

stages.title: Edge cases and complexity
stages.body:
✍️ O(n) time, O(1) space.
✍️ All non-alphanumeric → the inner loops stop at l == r → returns true.
- `tolower` on digits leaves them unchanged.

stages.title: Carry forward
stages.body:
✍️ Palindrome / symmetry → opposite ends, compare, move both.
✍️ Any inner skip loop must repeat the outer guard (`l < r`).

stages.title: Interview follow-ups
stages.body:
- *Allow deleting one character* (LeetCode 680): at the first mismatch, try skipping either side ([[str-palindrome-checks#one-deletion]]).
- *Longest palindromic substring* — expand around centers (Day 8).

siblings.title: Valid Palindrome II
siblings.maps: At the first mismatch you get one deletion: try skipping the left char or the right char.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ Can the string be a palindrome after deleting at most one character?
✍️ Brute: delete each position and check → O(n²).

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Before the first mismatch everything matched, so the deletion must be one of the two mismatching characters. Check s[l+1..r] or s[l..r−1] → O(n).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Walk inwards; on a mismatch return isPal(l+1, r) || isPal(l, r−1); if no mismatch, true.

stages.title: Pseudocode
Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ "At most one mistake allowed" → handle the first mistake both possible ways, then continue normally ([[str-palindrome-checks#one-deletion]]).

siblings.title: Reverse Vowels of a String
siblings.maps: Opposite ends that only stop on vowels — same skip-loop structure as Valid Palindrome.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Reverse only the vowels (both cases) of a string.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Move l to the next vowel, r to the previous vowel, swap, repeat.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Skip non-vowels on both sides (guarding l < r), swap, move inwards.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
while l < r:
    while l < r and not vowel(s[l]): l++
    while l < r and not vowel(s[r]): r--
    swap(s[l++], s[r--])
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ The skip-loop structure is reusable for any "act only on some characters" two-pointer problem.

siblings.title: Reverse Only Letters
siblings.maps: Identical shape with `isalpha` as the filter.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Reverse the letters, leaving every non-letter in place.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Opposite ends skipping non-letters; swap letters.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Same as reverse vowels with the filter "is a letter".

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
while l < r: skip non-letters on both sides; swap; move inwards
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Pattern recognition: if two problems differ only in the filter predicate, they are the same problem.

theory_refs.at: Fix one, the rest is sorted two-sum

theory_refs.why: Where to skip and why compare with the previous element.

stages.title: Understand
stages.body:
✍️ f(array) → all **unique** triplets [x, y, z] (values, not indices) with x + y + z = 0.
- n ≤ 3000 → O(n²) = 9·10⁶ is fine, O(n³) = 2.7·10¹⁰ is not.
- [−1, 0, 1, 2, −1, −4] → [[−1, −1, 2], [−1, 0, 1]].

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ Target: O(n²). Values are returned, not indices → sorting is allowed.
✍️ By hand: if I fix −1, I need two numbers summing to +1 — that is Two Sum II on the rest of the array.
✍️ Hard part: **unique** triplets. The input [−1, −1, 2] could produce [−1, −1, 2] twice from different −1s.
✍️ Edges: all zeros [0, 0, 0, 0] → one triplet; fewer than 3 elements; no solution.

stages.title: Brainstorm: brute → optimal
stages.body:
✍️ **1. Brute.** Three loops + a set of sorted triplets. O(n³) + dedup overhead.
✍️ ↳ Bottleneck: the inner two loops search for a pair with sum −a[i] — a 2-sum problem.
✍️ **2. Hash per i.** For each i, a hash-set two-sum on the rest. O(n²), but dedup is messy.
✍️ **3. Optimal.** Sort once. For each i: two pointers on i+1..n−1 looking for −a[i]. Dedup by skipping equal values (they are adjacent after sorting). O(n²), O(1) extra.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body:
✍️ 1. Sort the array.
✍️ 2. For each index i: skip it if a[i] equals a[i−1] (same first value → same triplets). Stop if a[i] > 0.
✍️ 3. Set l = i+1, r = n−1. While l < r: compute the sum. Too small → l++. Too big → r--.
✍️ 4. On a hit: record it, move both pointers, and skip over equal values on both sides.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
STATE   sort(a); res = []
LOOP    for i in 0..n-3
CHECK     if i > 0 and a[i] == a[i-1]: continue      ← dedup 1
          if a[i] > 0: break
          l = i+1; r = n-1
          while l < r:
              s = a[i] + a[l] + a[r]
              if s < 0: l++
              elif s > 0: r--
              else:
UPDATE            res.add([a[i], a[l], a[r]]); l++; r--
                  while l < r and a[l] == a[l-1]: l++   ← dedup 2
                  while l < r and a[r] == a[r+1]: r--   ← dedup 3
RETURN  res
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Edge cases and complexity
stages.body:
✍️ O(n²) time, O(1) extra (besides output and the sort).
✍️ Skipping on `a[i] == a[i+1]` (instead of `a[i−1]`) would skip the **first** −1 and lose [−1, −1, 2].
- [0, 0, 0, 0]: i = 0 finds [0, 0, 0]; the inner skips and i = 1.. are duplicates.

stages.title: Carry forward
stages.body:
✍️ k-sum → sort + fix k−2 elements + two pointers → O(n^(k−1)).
✍️ "Unique combinations of values" → sort, then skip equal neighbours instead of using a set.
✍️ Fixing one element turns an unfamiliar problem into a familiar one — a general strategy.

stages.title: Interview follow-ups
stages.body:
- *3Sum Closest* — same scan, track the best |sum − target|.
- *4Sum* — two outer loops + two pointers, `long long` sums.
- *Count triplets with sum < target* — when the sum is small enough, add r − l at once.
- *Can it be done in better than O(n²)?* Not in general (3SUM is believed to need ~n²); say so.

siblings.title: 3Sum Closest
siblings.maps: Same sorted scan, but instead of an exact hit you track the sum nearest the target.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Return the sum of three numbers closest to target (one answer).

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Brute O(n³). Sort + fix i + two pointers: the pointer moves are the same (too small → l++, too big → r−−); record whichever sum has the smallest |s − target|. No dedup needed.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Sort; for each i, scan with l and r, updating the best sum; return early on an exact match.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
sort a; best = a[0]+a[1]+a[2]
for i: l = i+1; r = n-1
    while l < r:
        s = a[i]+a[l]+a[r]
        if |s-t| < |best-t|: best = s
        if s < t: l++ elif s > t: r-- else: return s
return best
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ "Closest" versions keep the pointer logic and add a running best ([[tp-fix-one-k-sum#variations]]).

siblings.title: 4Sum
siblings.maps: One more fixed loop; dedup at both fixed levels; `long long` sums.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ All unique quadruplets summing to target; values up to 10⁹ → sums overflow int.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Sort; fix i and j (both with dedup); two pointers for the last two. O(n³).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Two outer loops with "skip equal to previous at this level", inner two-pointer scan with dedup after hits.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
for i: skip dup; for j > i: skip dup (j > i+1)
    l = j+1; r = n-1; two-pointer on long long sum
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Dedup guard at a nested level is `j > i + 1`, the start of that level ([[tp-skip-duplicates#pitfalls]]).

siblings.title: Valid Triangle Number
siblings.maps: Fix the largest side; on the rest, two pointers count a block of valid pairs at once.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Count triples that can form a triangle: for sorted a ≤ b ≤ c, need a + b > c.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Sort. For each c = a[k] (from the right), l = 0, r = k−1: if a[l] + a[r] > a[k], every l' in [l, r−1] also works with r → add r − l, r−−; else l++. O(n²).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Fix the largest side, count pairs on its left with the block trick.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
sort a; cnt = 0
for k from n-1 down to 2:
    l = 0; r = k-1
    while l < r:
        if a[l] + a[r] > a[k]: cnt += r - l; r--
        else: l++
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Fixing the **largest** element makes the condition a single inequality — choose what to fix so the rest is a known 2-pointer problem.

theory_refs.why: The formula the proof is built on.

theory_refs.at: Moving the taller wall never helps

theory_refs.why: The same proof style justifies greedy algorithms.

stages.title: Understand
stages.body:
✍️ f(heights h) → max over i < j of min(h[i], h[j]) × (j − i).
- n ≤ 10⁵ → O(n²) is too slow.
- [1,8,6,2,5,4,8,3,7] → 49 (walls at index 1 and 8: min(8,7) × 7).

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ This is a DISGUISE: it is not sorted, there is no target — yet it is opposite-end two pointers.
✍️ By hand: start with the widest container (both ends). To find something better I must lose width, so I need more height. The shorter wall caps the height — keeping it can never help.
✍️ Hard part: convincing yourself that discarding the shorter wall loses nothing.
✍️ Edges: n = 2; equal heights; heights of 0.

stages.title: Brainstorm: brute → optimal
stages.body:
✍️ **1. Brute.** All pairs. O(n²) → too slow at 10⁵.
✍️ ↳ Bottleneck: checking pairs that obviously cannot win.
✍️ ↳ Unlock: which pairs can be discarded safely? With l and r at the ends and h[l] < h[r], every pair (l, j) with j < r has smaller width and height ≤ h[l]. So l's best is already computed → discard l.
✍️ **2. Optimal.** l = 0, r = n−1. Record area, move the pointer at the **shorter** wall. O(n), O(1).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body:
✍️ 1. Pointers at both ends, best = 0.
✍️ 2. Compute the area of the current pair and update best.
✍️ 3. Move the pointer with the smaller height inward (either one if equal).
✍️ 4. Stop when they meet.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
STATE   l = 0; r = n-1; best = 0
LOOP    while l < r
UPDATE    best = max(best, min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l))
          if h[l] < h[r]: l++  else: r--
RETURN  best
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Edge cases and complexity
stages.body:
✍️ O(n) time, O(1) space.
- Max area ≤ 10⁴ × 10⁵ = 10⁹ fits in int.
- Equal heights: moving either is safe — both have already achieved their best.

stages.title: Carry forward
stages.body:
✍️ Two pointers work whenever you can prove one side is "done" after each comparison — sortedness is only one way to get that proof.
✍️ Learn the proof sentence; it is the interview answer ([[tp-why-discarding-is-safe#how-to-say]]).

stages.title: Interview follow-ups
stages.body:
- *Why not move the taller wall?* Width drops and height stays capped by the shorter wall.
- *Trapping Rain Water* (LeetCode 42) looks similar but sums water over every bar: two pointers with leftMax/rightMax, or prefix/suffix maxima ([[ps-prefix-suffix-passes]]).

siblings.title: Boats to Save People
siblings.maps: Opposite ends after sorting: the heaviest person boards now; take the lightest along if they fit.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Each boat carries at most 2 people with total weight ≤ limit. Minimum boats.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Sort. The heaviest person must go in some boat; the best partner is the lightest (if even the lightest doesn't fit, nobody does). Greedy with l, r → O(n log n).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Sort; while l ≤ r: if a[l] + a[r] ≤ limit, l++; always r−− and count a boat.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
sort a; l = 0; r = n-1; boats = 0
while l <= r:
    if a[l] + a[r] <= limit: l++
    r--; boats++
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body:
✍️ `l <= r` here (not `<`): one person alone still needs a boat.
✍️ The "heaviest with lightest" choice is justified by an exchange argument ([[gr-what-greedy-is-and-proofs#exchange]]).

siblings.title: Trapping Rain Water
siblings.maps: Water above bar i = min(maxLeft, maxRight) − h[i]; two pointers process the side with the smaller max.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ Total water trapped between bars after rain.
✍️ Brute: for each bar, scan left and right for maxima → O(n²).

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Prefix max + suffix max arrays → O(n) time, O(n) space ([[ps-prefix-suffix-passes]]). Two pointers: if leftMax < rightMax, the left bar's water is decided by leftMax (the right side has something at least as tall) → O(1) space.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Move the pointer whose running max is smaller; add (its max − its height) and update the max.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
l = 0; r = n-1; lm = rm = 0; water = 0
while l < r:
    if h[l] < h[r]: lm = max(lm, h[l]); water += lm - h[l]; l++
    else: rm = max(rm, h[r]); water += rm - h[r]; r--
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Same "the smaller side is decided" logic as Container With Most Water ([[tp-why-discarding-is-safe#container]]).

siblings.title: Max Number of K-Sum Pairs
siblings.maps: Sort + opposite ends; each exact hit removes both elements (moves both pointers).

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Repeatedly remove two numbers summing to k; maximum number of removals.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Sort + two pointers: hit → count++, l++, r−−; small → l++; big → r−−. (Hash-map counting also works in O(n).)

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Two-sum scan that keeps going after each hit.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
sort a; l = 0; r = n-1; ops = 0
while l < r:
    s = a[l] + a[r]
    if s == k: ops++; l++; r--
    elif s < k: l++ else: r--
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Pairing up greedily on sorted data is optimal for "maximum number of disjoint pairs with sum k".

drill.title: Check If N and Its Double Exist
drill.statement: Decide whether the array contains two different positions holding x and 2x.
drill.approach: Walk once with a set; for each x check whether 2x or x/2 (when x is even) was seen before, then insert x.
drill.trigger: "exists i ≠ j with a relation between a[i] and a[j]" on unsorted data → hash set.
drill.details:
**Task.** Are there two different indices i ≠ j such that `arr[i]` is exactly twice `arr[j]`?

**Input:** an integer array `arr`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 2 ≤ length ≤ 500; −1000 ≤ `arr[i]` ≤ 1000.

**Example:** `[10, 2, 5, 3]` → `true` (10 = 2 × 5). `[3, 1, 7, 11]` → `false`. `[0, 0]` → `true`, but `[0]` alone could never pair with itself.

drill.title: Backspace String Compare
drill.statement: Two strings where '#' means backspace; decide whether they produce the same text.
drill.pattern_name: Two pointers from the back (or a stack)
drill.approach: A stack builds each final string in O(n) space. For O(1): walk both strings from the end, skipping characters cancelled by pending backspaces, comparing the next real characters.
drill.trigger: "backspace / undo" → stack; "O(1) space" follow-up → pointers from the end.
drill.details:
**Task.** Each string is a sequence of keystrokes typed into an empty editor, where `#` is a backspace. Backspace on an empty editor does nothing. Do the two strings leave the same text?

**Input:** strings `s`, `t`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ lengths ≤ 200; lowercase letters and `#` only. Follow-up: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

**Example:** `"ab#c"`, `"ad#c"` → `true` (both give `"ac"`). `"a##c"`, `"#a#c"` → `true` (both give `"c"`). `"a#c"`, `"b"` → `false`.

drill.title: Is Subsequence
drill.statement: Decide whether s can be obtained from t by deleting some characters without reordering.
drill.pattern_name: Two pointers moving in the same direction
drill.approach: Pointer i in s, j in t; advance j always, advance i when s[i] == t[j]; true if i reaches the end of s.
drill.trigger: "subsequence check" between two sequences → greedy same-direction pointers.
drill.details:
**Task.** Can `s` be obtained from `t` by deleting zero or more characters of `t` without changing the order of the rest?

**Input:** strings `s`, `t`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 0 ≤ `s` length ≤ 100; 0 ≤ `t` length ≤ 10⁴; lowercase letters only. Follow-up: billions of different `s` strings against the same `t`.

**Example:** `"abc"`, `"ahbgdc"` → `true`. `"axc"`, `"ahbgdc"` → `false`.

drill.title: Minimum Difference Between Highest and Lowest of K Scores
drill.statement: Pick k scores so that the gap between the largest and smallest picked is as small as possible.
drill.approach: Sort; the best k always form a contiguous block in sorted order; answer = min over i of a[i+k−1] − a[i].
drill.trigger: "choose k elements minimising max − min" → sort, then the choice is a window.
drill.details:
**Task.** Choose any k students' scores from the array. Make the difference between the highest and lowest chosen score as small as possible, and return that difference.

**Input:** an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ k ≤ length ≤ 1000; 0 ≤ `nums[i]` ≤ 10⁵.

**Example:** `[9, 4, 1, 7]`, k = 2 → `2`. Choosing 9 and 7 gives 2, and no pair is closer. `[90]`, k = 1 → `0`.

drill.title: Long Pressed Name
drill.statement: A friend typed a name, but some keys may have been held down and repeated. Decide whether the typed text could come from the name.
drill.approach: Pointer i in name, j in typed; if characters match advance both; else if typed[j] repeats typed[j−1] advance j; else false. At the end i must reach the end of name.
drill.trigger: comparing two sequences where one may contain extra repeats → two forward pointers.
drill.details:
**Task.** Your friend typed their name, but some keys may have been held down, so a character may appear one or more extra times in a row. Could `typed` be the result of typing `name` this way?

**Input:** strings `name`, `typed`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ lengths ≤ 1000; lowercase letters only.

**Example:** `"alex"`, `"aaleex"` → `true`. `"saeed"`, `"ssaaedd"` → `false`: the second e is missing, and the extra d does not belong.

sections.title: Concept
sections.body:
✍️ **Inheritance** lets a class (derived/child) reuse and extend another class (base/parent). It models an **is-a** relationship: a `SavingsAccount` is an `Account`.
✍️ Access in C++: `class D : public B` keeps public as public and protected as protected (the normal choice). `protected`/`private` inheritance hides the base's interface.
✍️ Construction order: base constructor first, then derived. Destruction: derived destructor first, then base.
✍️ Types: single, multiple (`class D : public A, public B`), multilevel (A → B → C), hierarchical (many children of one parent), hybrid.

sections.title: C++ example
Interview questions
sections.body:
✍️ **Q: What is the diamond problem?** With multiple inheritance, D inherits from B and C which both inherit from A → D gets two copies of A, and calls to A's members are ambiguous. C++ fixes it with **virtual inheritance** (`class B : virtual public A`) so only one A exists. Java avoids it by forbidding multiple class inheritance (interfaces only).
✍️ **Q: Is-a vs has-a?** Inheritance models is-a; **composition** (a member object) models has-a (a Car has an Engine). Prefer composition when the relationship is not truly is-a.
✍️ **Q: What is not inherited?** Constructors (unless `using Base::Base`), destructors, assignment operators and friends.
- **Q: Can a derived class access private members of the base?** No — only protected and public ones.

micro.title: Two pointers — let sorted order tell you which way to move

sections.title: Micro-theory (10 minutes)
sections.body:
Yesterday's Two Sum needed a hash map because the array was unsorted. When the array is **sorted**, the order itself tells you which direction improves the answer — and you need no extra memory.

✍️ Put `l` at the start and `r` at the end. Compare, then move exactly one pointer. Each move throws away a whole set of pairs that provably cannot work → O(n) ([[tp-opposite-ends#idea]]).
✍️ Learn the one-line proof, because interviewers ask for it: "if `a[l] + a[r] < target`, every pair using `l` is too small, so `l` is useless" ([[tp-why-discarding-is-safe#argument]]).
✍️ For three numbers: sort, fix the first, two-pointer the rest ([[tp-fix-one-k-sum#idea]]), and skip duplicates by comparing with the previous element ([[tp-skip-duplicates#idioms]]).
- Sorting: `sort(a.begin(), a.end())`, O(n log n) ([[cpp-sort-and-comparators#basics]]).

sections.title: Pattern card
sections.body:
✍️ OPPOSITE ENDS — trigger: sorted + pair, or palindrome/symmetry, or "O(1) space". `while (l < r)`: too small → l++, too big → r--.
✍️ WHY SAFE — the pointer you move cannot be part of any better answer.
✍️ K-SUM — sort; for i: skip a[i]==a[i−1]; two pointers on i+1..n−1; after a hit move both and skip equal neighbours.
